ety.text: From Middle English rop, rope, from Old English rāp (“rope, cord, cable”), from Proto-West Germanic *raip, from Proto-Germanic *raipaz, *raipą (“rope, cord, band, ringlet”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁roypnós (“strap, band, rope”), from *h₁reyp- (“to peel off, tear; border, edge, strip”).
From Middle English ropen, rope (“to form ropes”), from rop (“rope”); see above.
From Middle English rop (“gut, intestine”), from Old English rop, ropp; compare Middle Dutch rop, roppe (“fish guts”). The modern pronunciation results from phonological assimilation to Etymology 1.

senses.d: Thick strings, yarn, monofilaments, metal wires, or strands of other cordage that are twisted together to form a stronger line.
ex: Nylon rope is usually stronger than similar rope made of plant fibers.

senses.d: An individual length of such material.
ex: The swinging bridge is constructed of 40 logs and 30 ropes.
All at once, let’s heave on the rope!
The duchess wore a rope of pearls to the soirée.
Jimmy began to scream and ropes of spit shot from his mouth.
The principle of any such device should be to pull on the vessel by a rope of water passing in at the bow and out at the stern.
He hit a rope past third and into the corner.

senses.d: A long thin segment of soft clay, either extruded or formed by hand.
A data structure resembling a string, using a concatenation tree in which each leaf represents a character.
A kind of chaff (material dropped to interfere with radar) consisting of foil strips with paper chutes attached.
A unit of distance equivalent to the distance covered in six months by a god flying at ten million miles per second.
A necklace of at least one meter in length.
To throw a rope (or something similar, e.g. a lasso, cable, wire, etc.) around (something).
To climb by means of a rope or ropes.
ex: We roped down to the platform selected for the bivouac; set up our bags and brewed a reasonable meal.

senses.d: To be formed into rope; to draw out or extend into a filament or thread.
ex: Let us not hang like roping icicles / Upon our houses' thatch.

senses.d: To pull or restrain (the horse one is riding) to prevent it from winning a race.
ex: Others, a shade more advanced, have been known to bribe a jockey to "hold," "rope" a horse, or a stableman to poison or stupefy him.

senses.d: To commit suicide, particularly by hanging.
ex: My life is a mess; I might as well rope.
In figure 71, the poster Brahcel notes that he “almost roped” because he could not find the community […]

ety.text: From Vulgar Latin, Late Latin sōca, of Celtic origin, from Gaulish *soukā, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sew- (“to bend, to cut, to drive”), see also Sanskrit सुवति (suvati). Compare Portuguese and Asturian soga, Italian soga, French suage, Friulian soe, Romansh suga, Venetan soga.
